prompt: Write a recommendation letter from a machine learning professor for an undergraduate applying to a research master's program in artificial intelligence.
gpt_text: Dear Admissions Committee, I am pleased to recommend Maya Singh for your research master's program in artificial intelligence. Maya worked with me for two semesters in my machine learning laboratory, where she investigated calibration methods for neural classifiers under distribution shift. She combines mathematical maturity with a patient experimental style that is rare in undergraduate researchers. When an initial set of results contradicted our expectations, Maya traced the discrepancy to a subtle data preprocessing issue and then redesigned the evaluation protocol with impressive care. She is also a generous collaborator who improves the work of people around her. I believe she has the independence, rigor, and curiosity to thrive in a demanding research environment, and I recommend her with enthusiasm.

prompt: Draft a talk proposal by a computer science professor for a departmental seminar on trustworthy large language models.
gpt_text: Title: Toward Trustworthy Large Language Models in Open-Ended Settings. This talk will examine why reliability remains difficult even as language models become more capable. I will focus on three linked challenges: measuring factuality when tasks are underspecified, designing retrieval and verification pipelines that expose uncertainty, and evaluating models in high-stakes workflows where human oversight is uneven. Rather than presenting trustworthiness as a single metric, I will argue for a layered view that combines model behavior, interface design, institutional safeguards, and domain expertise. The talk will include recent experimental findings from my group on selective generation and abstention, followed by open questions for faculty and students interested in responsible AI deployment.

prompt: Write a short article by a professor explaining recent advances in multimodal machine learning for a university newsletter.
gpt_text: Multimodal machine learning has moved from a specialized research area to one of the central directions in artificial intelligence. Modern systems can now connect text, images, audio, video, and structured data in ways that make interaction more natural and analysis more flexible. The most important shift is not simply that models can label pictures or transcribe speech, but that they can reason across sources: a diagram can be discussed in language, a video can be searched by concept, and a scientific figure can be interpreted alongside its caption. These capabilities raise important questions about evaluation, bias, and provenance. In our department, we see multimodal AI as both a technical frontier and a chance to build tools that help people understand complex information more effectively.

prompt: Compose a nomination letter from a computer science professor for a doctoral student being considered for a university teaching award.
gpt_text: Dear Awards Committee, I am delighted to nominate Daniel Okafor for the Graduate Teaching Excellence Award. Daniel served as head teaching assistant for Algorithms and Data Structures, a course with more than 250 students and a wide range of preparation levels. He transformed our discussion sections by replacing routine problem walkthroughs with carefully staged reasoning exercises that helped students see how algorithmic ideas emerge. Student evaluations repeatedly praised his clarity, fairness, and calm presence during a demanding term. Just as important, Daniel mentored junior teaching assistants, created reusable grading rubrics, and identified accessibility improvements for our online materials. His teaching reflects both intellectual precision and deep respect for students, and he is exceptionally deserving of this recognition.

prompt: Write a research statement excerpt from a machine learning professor applying for a faculty position in computer science.
gpt_text: My research develops machine learning systems that remain reliable when the world changes around them. Much of modern AI assumes that training and deployment data are drawn from similar distributions, yet real systems encounter new users, new sensors, new language, and new incentives. My work addresses this gap through methods for uncertainty estimation, adaptive evaluation, and human-centered model monitoring. I am especially interested in the boundary between statistical robustness and institutional trust: when should a model defer, ask for more context, or expose the evidence behind its prediction? Looking ahead, my lab will build learning systems that combine strong empirical performance with transparent failure modes, enabling safer use in science, education, and public-interest applications.

prompt: Draft a letter from a professor to an industry partner proposing a collaborative project on privacy-preserving federated learning.
gpt_text: Dear Dr. Alvarez, I am writing to propose a collaboration between our machine learning group and your applied analytics team on privacy-preserving federated learning. Your organization faces exactly the kind of setting where data are valuable but difficult to centralize: distributed clients, heterogeneous usage patterns, and legitimate privacy constraints. We would like to study algorithms that improve personalization while limiting the movement of raw data. The project could begin with a three-month feasibility phase in which we define a representative task, establish privacy and evaluation requirements, and test baseline federated optimization methods. My students would contribute methodological expertise, while your team would provide domain constraints and deployment insight. I believe this partnership could produce both publishable research and practical guidance for responsible machine learning infrastructure.

prompt: Write a concise peer review by a professor for a machine learning conference paper on graph neural networks.
gpt_text: This paper proposes a message-passing architecture for graph neural networks that incorporates adaptive neighborhood selection. The main idea is interesting and potentially useful, especially for graphs with noisy or weakly informative edges. The experiments show consistent gains on several benchmark datasets, and the ablation study suggests that the adaptive component contributes meaningfully to performance. However, the paper would be stronger with a clearer discussion of computational cost and scalability. The current comparison focuses primarily on accuracy, while training time and memory usage are only briefly mentioned. I would also like to see evaluation on at least one large, real-world graph where neighborhood sampling is essential. Overall, I view the submission as a promising contribution that requires some additional evidence to fully support its claims.

prompt: Compose a short email from a professor inviting a distinguished researcher to give a keynote lecture at an AI workshop.
gpt_text: Dear Professor Chen, I hope this message finds you well. I am writing on behalf of the organizing committee for the Workshop on Human-Centered AI Systems, to be held this October at Northbridge University. We would be honored if you would consider giving the keynote lecture. Your work on interactive machine learning and model accountability has shaped many of the questions this workshop hopes to address, particularly how technical design choices affect users, institutions, and public trust. The keynote would be scheduled for 45 minutes with 15 minutes for discussion, and we would be pleased to cover travel and lodging. Please let me know if you might be available, and I would be happy to provide additional details.

prompt: Write a lab policy memo from a machine learning professor about responsible use of generative AI tools in research.
gpt_text: Lab members may use generative AI tools to support research activities such as brainstorming, editing, code review, and summarizing background material. However, these tools must not replace independent verification, careful reading, or accountable authorship. Any factual claim, citation, theorem statement, dataset description, or experimental result produced with AI assistance must be checked against primary sources or our own records. Generated code should be reviewed with the same care as code written by a collaborator, including tests and attention to licensing. Do not upload confidential data, unpublished manuscripts, private reviewer comments, or restricted human-subjects material to external systems without explicit approval. When AI tools materially shape a manuscript, presentation, or analysis pipeline, document that use transparently in the project notes.

prompt: Draft a recommendation letter from a computer science professor for a master's student applying to a software engineering role focused on machine learning infrastructure.
gpt_text: To Whom It May Concern, I am happy to recommend Leo Martinez for the machine learning infrastructure position at your company. Leo completed my graduate course in Scalable Machine Learning Systems and later joined my group as a project assistant. His strongest quality is the ability to bridge algorithmic understanding with careful engineering. In one project, he redesigned a training pipeline so that experiments became reproducible across machines, with clear configuration files, versioned datasets, and automated evaluation reports. He also communicates tradeoffs clearly, which is essential in infrastructure work where correctness, speed, and maintainability must be balanced. Leo is dependable, thoughtful, and technically mature. I believe he would contribute quickly to a team building robust ML systems.

prompt: Write a short article by a professor for the public about why evaluation is one of the hardest problems in artificial intelligence.
gpt_text: It is tempting to think that artificial intelligence improves whenever benchmark scores rise. Benchmarks are useful, but they are only partial maps of a much larger territory. Evaluation is hard because AI systems are increasingly used for open-ended tasks: drafting explanations, assisting decisions, analyzing images, and interacting with people in varied contexts. A model may perform well on a test set yet fail when instructions are ambiguous, data are incomplete, or users rely on it too heavily. Good evaluation therefore asks more than whether the answer is correct. It asks what evidence was used, how uncertainty was communicated, who might be harmed by mistakes, and whether the system supports responsible human judgment. In AI, measurement is not a final step; it is part of the design problem.

prompt: Compose a grant abstract by a computer science professor for a project on causal representation learning.
gpt_text: This project investigates causal representation learning for machine learning systems that must generalize beyond their training environments. Standard predictive models often rely on correlations that change across populations, institutions, or measurement conditions. The proposed research will develop methods for learning representations that capture stable causal structure while separating nuisance variation. The project combines theoretical analysis, synthetic benchmarks with known interventions, and applied studies in scientific data analysis. A central goal is to build models that can explain not only what they predict, but which relationships are expected to persist under plausible shifts. The work will train graduate and undergraduate researchers at the intersection of machine learning, causal inference, and responsible deployment, and will produce open-source tools for evaluating causal robustness.

prompt: Write feedback from a professor to a PhD student on a draft dissertation chapter about reinforcement learning.
gpt_text: This chapter has a strong core, especially in the way it connects policy optimization to the practical constraints of your robotics experiments. The motivation is now much clearer than in the previous draft. I suggest three revisions before we circulate it to the committee. First, move the discussion of reward shaping earlier, since it explains several design choices that otherwise appear ad hoc. Second, distinguish more explicitly between instability caused by exploration and instability caused by function approximation. Third, shorten the literature review by grouping related methods rather than summarizing each paper in sequence. The final experimental section is persuasive, but the figures need more consistent captions so readers can understand the comparison without returning to the main text.

prompt: Draft a short conference rebuttal by a professor responding to reviewers of a paper on uncertainty estimation.
gpt_text: We thank the reviewers for their careful reading and constructive comments. Several reviewers asked whether the proposed uncertainty estimates remain calibrated under distribution shift. In the revision, we will add an experiment on shifted image corruptions and a second experiment on temporal drift in tabular data. Preliminary results show that our method preserves lower calibration error than the strongest baseline in both settings, although performance degrades under severe shift. We will make that limitation explicit. Reviewer 2 noted that the method resembles temperature scaling; we will clarify that our approach learns input-dependent correction terms, while temperature scaling applies a global adjustment. We will also expand the computational cost discussion and release code for all reported experiments.

prompt: Write a formal letter from a professor supporting a student's application for a national fellowship in computing.
gpt_text: Dear Fellowship Committee, I strongly support Aisha Rahman's application for the National Fellowship in Computing. Aisha's research examines fairness in predictive models used for public services, and her work combines technical sophistication with a clear sense of civic responsibility. In my seminar on Responsible Machine Learning, she produced one of the best projects I have seen in recent years: a careful analysis of how missing data mechanisms can distort fairness metrics. She has since extended that work into a manuscript that is nearing submission. Aisha is independent without being isolated; she seeks critique early, revises thoughtfully, and contributes generously to our research community. I believe she has the promise to become a leader in socially grounded computer science research.

prompt: Compose a workshop call for papers written by a professor organizing an event on AI for scientific discovery.
gpt_text: We invite submissions to the Workshop on AI for Scientific Discovery, a forum for researchers developing machine learning methods that accelerate, challenge, or transform scientific practice. Topics of interest include foundation models for scientific data, simulation and surrogate modeling, active learning for experimentation, causal discovery, uncertainty quantification, interpretable models for domain experts, and evaluation protocols for AI-assisted research. We welcome full papers, short papers, position papers, and reports of negative results that clarify methodological limitations. Submissions should emphasize both technical contribution and scientific context. The workshop aims to bring together computer scientists, statisticians, and domain researchers for substantive discussion of how AI systems can support reliable discovery rather than merely optimize benchmark performance.

prompt: Write a note from a professor to students introducing a new graduate seminar on machine learning systems.
gpt_text: Welcome to Machine Learning Systems. This seminar is about the practical and conceptual machinery that turns models into usable systems: data pipelines, training infrastructure, evaluation, monitoring, deployment, and failure analysis. We will read papers from machine learning, databases, distributed systems, human-computer interaction, and software engineering. The central question is not only how to train a strong model, but how to build an environment in which the model's behavior can be understood, reproduced, improved, and governed. Students will lead discussions, write short critiques, and complete a final project that studies a real system design problem. I expect active participation, careful reading, and a willingness to connect elegant algorithms with the less elegant realities of operation.

prompt: Draft an award citation by a computer science professor for a colleague's contributions to programming languages and machine learning.
gpt_text: Professor Elena Park is recognized for outstanding contributions at the intersection of programming languages and machine learning. Her research has shown how ideas from type systems, program synthesis, and formal verification can make learning-enabled software more reliable and easier to reason about. She has developed influential frameworks for specifying behavioral constraints in data-driven systems and for detecting subtle failures in generated code. Beyond her technical contributions, Professor Park has built bridges between communities that too often work in parallel. Her papers are valued not only for their results, but for the clarity with which they identify shared problems. This award honors her originality, intellectual leadership, and lasting impact on modern computer science.

prompt: Write a short op-ed by a professor about the role of computer science education in the age of AI assistants.
gpt_text: AI assistants will change computer science education, but they do not make it obsolete. If anything, they sharpen the need to teach fundamentals well. Students still need to understand algorithms, systems, data, abstraction, and the social consequences of technology, because these are the tools that allow them to judge whether an automated suggestion is sensible. The classroom should not pretend that AI tools do not exist. Instead, we should teach students how to use them critically: to ask better questions, test generated code, identify unsupported claims, and reflect on authorship. The goal of computer science education is not to produce people who can type syntax from memory. It is to produce people who can reason carefully about computation in the world.

prompt: Compose a thesis examination report by a professor for a master's thesis on adversarial examples in deep learning.
gpt_text: The thesis provides a clear and competent study of adversarial examples in deep neural networks, with particular attention to image classification models. The student demonstrates a solid command of the relevant literature and implements several standard attack and defense methods. The strongest part of the work is the empirical comparison across perturbation budgets, where the analysis avoids overstating the effectiveness of any single defense. The thesis would benefit from a deeper discussion of threat models and from more explicit connections to real deployment settings. Nevertheless, the experimental work is careful, the writing is organized, and the conclusions are appropriately cautious. I recommend that the thesis be accepted, subject to minor revisions addressing the points above.

prompt: Write an email from a professor to a department chair proposing a new undergraduate course on data ethics and machine learning.
gpt_text: Dear Chair Williams, I would like to propose a new undergraduate course titled Data Ethics and Machine Learning for the next academic year. Our students are increasingly building systems that affect hiring, lending, health, education, and public administration, yet many encounter ethical and social questions only in scattered parts of the curriculum. This course would combine technical material on data collection, bias, privacy, interpretability, and evaluation with case studies and writing assignments. It would be suitable for juniors and seniors who have completed an introductory machine learning or data science course. I believe it would fill an important gap in our program and complement our existing offerings in AI, security, and human-centered computing. I would be glad to draft a full syllabus for discussion.

prompt: Compose a policy brief by a professor advising a university committee on procurement of generative AI tools.
gpt_text: The university should evaluate generative AI tools through a procurement process that considers privacy, accessibility, security, pedagogical value, and long-term governance. Cost and feature lists are insufficient. Any approved tool should provide clear data retention terms, administrative controls, auditability, and options for users who cannot or do not wish to use automated systems. The committee should distinguish between low-risk uses, such as drafting practice materials, and high-risk uses, such as grading, advising, or processing sensitive student records. Faculty and students need guidance on disclosure, acceptable use, and verification of generated content. I recommend a staged pilot with technical review, classroom evaluation, and an annual reassessment rather than a campus-wide commitment based on short-term enthusiasm.

prompt: Draft a short article by a computer science professor about why reproducibility matters in machine learning research.
gpt_text: Reproducibility is not clerical work; it is part of scientific reasoning. In machine learning, small implementation choices can change results: data splits, preprocessing, random seeds, hyperparameter searches, hardware libraries, and evaluation scripts all matter. When a result cannot be reproduced, the community loses the ability to distinguish a genuine idea from an accidental configuration. Reproducibility also helps researchers build on one another's work more efficiently. Clear code, documented experiments, and transparent reporting reduce wasted effort and make negative findings more informative. Perfect reproducibility is not always possible, especially for very large models or proprietary datasets, but that is not an excuse for opacity. The aim is to make the path from claim to evidence as inspectable as we reasonably can.

prompt: Write a professor's invitation to students for a reading group on foundation models and society.
gpt_text: I am starting a reading group this semester on foundation models and society, and interested graduate students are warmly invited to participate. We will meet every other Friday to discuss papers on model scaling, data governance, labor, evaluation, safety, regulation, and the changing organization of research. The group is intended to be interdisciplinary, so students from computer science, information science, statistics, law, and the social sciences are welcome. Each meeting will have one student discussion leader and a short written response circulated in advance. The goal is not to decide whether foundation models are simply good or bad, but to develop sharper ways of understanding their technical capabilities, institutional contexts, and social consequences.

prompt: Compose an internal memo by a professor about mentoring expectations for graduate students in a computer science lab.
gpt_text: Effective mentoring is a shared responsibility, but faculty must set clear expectations. Each graduate student in the lab should have a regular meeting schedule, written near-term goals, and at least one longer conversation each semester about research direction, professional development, and well-being. Students should receive timely feedback on papers, talks, and experimental plans, and they should know which decisions they can make independently. Mentoring should also include support for career paths beyond the narrowest version of academic success. I expect senior students and postdocs to contribute to a respectful intellectual environment, but supervision cannot be delegated entirely to them. Our lab should be ambitious without being opaque, demanding without being careless, and collaborative without making students guess what success requires.

prompt: Write a short project description by a professor for undergraduate researchers joining a computer vision lab.
gpt_text: This project studies how computer vision models behave when visual context changes in subtle but important ways. Many image classifiers perform well on standard benchmarks yet become unreliable when lighting, background, camera angle, or object co-occurrence differs from the training set. Undergraduate researchers will help build controlled evaluation datasets, run experiments with pretrained vision models, and analyze the kinds of mistakes those models make. Students will learn practical skills in Python, dataset documentation, experiment tracking, and scientific communication. Prior experience with deep learning is helpful but not required; curiosity, reliability, and careful attention to detail are more important. The broader aim is to understand how visual recognition systems can become more robust and more honestly evaluated.

prompt: Draft a professor's response to a student asking whether they should pursue a PhD in machine learning.
gpt_text: Dear Jordan, A PhD can be deeply rewarding, but it is worth choosing for the right reasons. It is not simply an advanced credential or a longer version of coursework. It is an apprenticeship in asking research questions, tolerating uncertainty, revising ideas, and working for long stretches without obvious external validation. You seem to enjoy open-ended technical problems, and your project this semester showed real independence, which are good signs. Before deciding, I encourage you to spend more time in a research group, talk with current doctoral students, and think honestly about what kinds of work energize you. If you want to create new knowledge and can imagine living with ambiguous problems for several years, a PhD may be a strong fit.
